extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of sociology/political philosophy (undergraduate/graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the parallels and differences between human societies and biological organisms as set out in a sociological/textbook treatment. The page lists specific points of similarity and difference and explains stages of social evolution (aggregation, differentiation, division of labour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commencement as small aggregations and insensible growth in mass
rubrics_metrics.description: "That commencing as small aggregations, they insensibly augment in mass: some of them eventually reaching ten thousand times what they originally were."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as societies starting small and growing greatly in size over time; compared to organisms that increase in mass during existence. Emphasizes gradual, not instantaneous, enlargement as a key parallelism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive increase in structural complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: "While at first so simple in structure as to be considered structureless, they assume, in the course of their growth, a continually-increasing complexity of structure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Societies move from simple to complex organization as they evolve; analogous to organisms developing specialized structures. The text links this to tiers of civilization and to biological developmental stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual acquisition of mutual dependence of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Though in their early, undeveloped states, there exists in them scarcely any mutual dependence of parts, their parts gradually acquire a mutual dependence; which becomes at last so great, that the activity and life of each part is made possible only by the activity and life of the rest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual interdependence among social parts increases with complexity, mirroring functional interdependence of organs in organisms. The loss or removal of significant parts causes great disturbance, especially in complex societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal life is independent of and outlives component units
rubrics_metrics.description: "The life of a society is independent of, and far more prolonged than, the lives of any of its component units; who are severally born, grow, work, reproduce, and die, while the body-politic composed of them survives generation after generation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Societies persist across generations even as individual members are born and die; continuity is maintained through replacement of units while the whole increases in mass and functional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of specific external form in societies
rubrics_metrics.description: "That societies have no specific external forms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is qualified: many organisms (especially lower plants/animals) also show indefinite forms and both social and biological forms are influenced by surrounding physical conditions. The point notes a contrast but downplays its absolute importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuity of living elements (dispersion vs continuous mass)
rubrics_metrics.description: "While the living tissue whereof an individual organism consists, forms a continuous mass, the living elements of a society do not form a continuous mass; but are more or less widely dispersed over some portion of the Earth's surface."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualification: human members are dispersed but inhabit a surface covered with lower-order life (vegetation, fauna) that supports social life; when that lower life is included, the apparent discontinuity is lessened. The social organism concept should include the supporting lower organic existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locomotion of social units versus fixed elements in organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ultimate living-elements of an individual organism are mostly fixed in their relative positions, those of the social organism are capable of moving from place to place."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualified: citizens may be locomotive privately but are stationary in public capacities (centres of production, firms, districts persist across generations). Therefore individual mobility does not invalidate the analogy to organismal fixedness of functional positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal sensitiveness in societies versus localized nervous system
rubrics_metrics.description: "While in the body of an animal only a special tissue is endowed with feelings, in a society all the members are endowed with feeling."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualification: sensitivity varies by class (laboring classes less intellectually/emotionally susceptible). Crucial implication: societies lack a corporate consciousness; thus individual welfare cannot rightly be sacrificed to a supposed benefit of the State — the community should exist for the benefit of citizens, not vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive division of labour (physiological division of labour)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that, as societies evolve, there is a progressive subdivision and specialization of functions analogous to physiological differentiation in organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links economic division of labour to physiological division; specialization produces mutually dependent parts. Cites embryological parallels (endoderm/ectoderm) as foundational divisions leading to alimentary vs external action functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary differentiation analogous to embryonic germ layers (governing vs governed)
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary social differentiation corresponds to the embryo's endoderm/ectoderm: an upper/governing class (external action) and a lower/working class (alimentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The warrior/governing class performs external acts (war, negotiation, migration) and later becomes regulative/defensive; the lower class provides material necessities (alimentation). The analogy underlies future social structure and specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationarity of social organs despite turnover of persons
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each great centre of production, each manufacturing town or district, continues always in the same place; and many of the firms in such town or district are for generations carried on either by the descendants or successors of those who founded them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social 'organs' (institutions, firms, production centers) persist as functional units even though the individuals composing them change, paralleling cellular replacement within an organ of an organism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication, division, and coalescence of groups into larger political units
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes by which small tribes or communities divide (migration, fission) or coalesce (fusion, subjugation), ultimately forming nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains analogies to budding and compound animals (Hydra, Polyzoa): as tribes grow too large or face resource limits they split; where migration is constrained, kindred communities remain in contact and fuse into nations. Cites Guizot on formation of broader political authority.
